original_summary: Medici is a 2-6 player auction game over 3 days. Each turn the active player turns up 1-3 commodity cards as a lot, which is then auctioned once around the table. Players load the lots onto ships of limited size and score florins for ship value rankings and commodity majorities; the most florins wins.

review.evidence: Always passing earns no ship or commodity income. Always bidding high bankrupts a player early. Lot size, overfill limits and turn order create real choices. The fixed once-around order does give the drawer a last-bid edge, but it rotates.
Valuing a lot against ship space, money left and majority races is a skill. Experienced players beat novices fairly reliably, though the order of the deck adds noticeable swing.
Pricing, timing lot sizes to starve rivals, and reading who can still bid give deep play. A weak player still picks up some cheap lots and scores.

Cards are face-up and the state is almost fully public. The inference lies in reading opponents' valuations and budgets. No player holds a private goal, so there is little hidden information to infer.
All scoring is arithmetic on card values, counts and florins.

The commodity track is a small board. The draw-1-to-3 loop needs several random draws per turn. The day length depends on ships filling. The clockwise auction needs one choice step per player, which can exceed 4 choice steps. Ranking ships over 6 players needs costly arithmetic.

problems: P1: Drawing cards one at a time with a stop decision needs up to 3 random draws and nested choices per turn, which exceeds the limit of 1 random draw per round.
P2: The clockwise once-around auction needs one sequential choice step per player, which exceeds 4 choice steps with 5-6 players.
P3: The day ends when ships fill, which is a variable, conditional length that is hard to build and to balance.
P4: The game is nearly perfect-information, with no private goal, so there is little to infer beyond rivals' money.
P5: The commodity track is a board, and full ship rankings over many players need expensive ranking arithmetic.
P6: A wide player range (2-6) makes the deck size, the number of rounds and seat parity hard to keep fair.

changes.what: Shuffle the deck once at the start of each day. Each round, reveal the top 3 cards, and the active player chooses to auction the first 1, 2 or all 3.
changes.why: This keeps the drawer's lot-size decision while using one shuffle per day and no random draw in other rounds.

changes.what: Replace the once-around auction with a single sealed simultaneous bid from every player. Ties go to the active player, then to the tied player next in seating order after the active player.
changes.why: This takes one choice step regardless of player count. Bluffing and valuation stay central, and the drawer keeps a tie edge in place of the last-bid edge.

changes.what: Each day has exactly 2 lots per player (8 rounds with 4 players). Ships hold 5 cards, and a player whose ship lacks room cannot win the lot.
changes.why: A fixed length gives each seat equal active turns and needs no variable day ending. Capacity still bites.

changes.what: Each player is secretly dealt a different favoured good, worth 3 extra florins per card of it collected over the game.
changes.why: This adds a hidden private goal. Bids leak information about it, so players must infer rivals' goals and can disguise their own by bidding on decoys. All goods have identical card distributions, so the deal is worth the same to everyone.

changes.what: Replace the commodity track with per-player running counts per good and an end-game majority bonus. Replace the full ship ranking with a top-two bonus each day.
changes.why: This keeps majority races and ship-value competition using simple counts and max calculations.

changes.what: Limit the game to 3-4 players, with a 48-card deck reshuffled each day.
changes.why: The deck always covers a day's reveals, and the round counts give every seat equal turns.

keeps: Auctioning lots of commodity cards for florins
The active player choosing how big a lot to offer
Limited ship capacity, where a lot that would overfill your ship cannot be won
Three days with a ship-value bonus each day and ships emptied between days
Commodity majority racing across the whole game
Most florins at the end wins

recommendation.reason: The auction-valuation core is strong reasoning material. It fits once bids are sealed, lengths are fixed and a hidden favoured good is added.

variation.name: Medici: Sealed Ledgers
variation.summary: Players bid sealed florins for lots of commodity cards over 3 days. They fill 5-card ships for daily value bonuses, race for commodity majorities, and chase a secret favoured good that rivals try to read from their bids.
variation.rules:
SETUP. Each player starts with 40 florins. Florin totals are private to each player, and the engine tracks them. The deck has 48 cards: 4 goods (Grain, Cloth, Spice, Dye) with 12 cards each. Each good has the card values 0,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,5,5. Each player is secretly dealt a different favoured good, chosen at random from the 4, and only that player knows it. Seats are numbered 1 to N. The active player in round r is seat ((r-1) mod N)+1.

DAYS AND ROUNDS. The game lasts 3 days. Each day has 2N rounds: 6 rounds with 3 players, 8 with 4. The game therefore has 6N rounds in total (18 or 24). At the start of each day, all 48 cards are shuffled into a fresh deck, and every ship is empty. A ship holds at most 5 cards.

EACH ROUND:
1. Reveal. The top 3 cards of the deck are revealed to everyone, in order, as cards A, B and C.
2. Lot size. The active player chooses 1, 2 or 3. The lot is card A, cards A and B, or cards A, B and C. Unchosen revealed cards are discarded. The lot is announced.
3. Sealed bids. All players, including the active player, at the same moment secretly bid a whole number of florins from 0 up to their own current florins. A bid of 0 is a pass.
4. Validity. A bid is treated as 0 if loading the lot would put that player's ship over 5 cards.
5. Winner. The highest valid bid above 0 wins. Ties go to the active player if tied. Otherwise they go to the tied player who comes first in seating order starting after the active player. If every bid is 0, the lot is discarded.
6. Payment and loading. The winner pays the bid to the bank and loads the lot onto their ship. The winner's ship value rises by the sum of the lot's card values. Their ship card count rises by the lot size. Their game-long count of each good rises by the number of cards of that good in the lot.
7. Announcement. The engine announces the winner, the price paid, and every player's ship card count. It does not announce florin totals.

END OF DAY (after the last round of each day):
- The highest ship value earns 15 florins. The second-highest earns 7. If several players tie for highest, they split 22 florins equally, rounded down, and no second place is paid. If several tie for second, they split 7 equally, rounded down. A ship value of 0 earns nothing.
- Then all ships are emptied: value 0, card count 0. The game-long good counts are kept.

END OF GAME (after day 3 scoring):
- Majorities. For each good, the player with the most cards of it over the whole game earns 10 florins. Ties split 10 equally, rounded down. If nobody has any cards of a good, nothing is paid for it.
- Favoured good. Each player earns 3 florins per card of their own favoured good collected over the game. Favoured goods are then revealed.

There is no talk phase.
variation.objective: After the end-of-game scoring, the player with the most florins wins. If several tie for most, the tied player with more total cards collected over the game wins. If still tied, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Sealed bids force players to price each lot against ship space, remaining money, the daily top-two race and majority races. The active player sizes lots to bundle junk with prizes or to fill a rival's ship. Every bid leaks information about a player's secret favoured good, so strong players infer rivals' goals and avoid bidding wars over them. They can also bid on a decoy good to mislead, which carries real cost because majorities pay. Simple policies lose. Always passing ends at 40 florins while active buyers net far more, since about 66 florins of daily bonuses plus 40 of majorities plus favoured-good income enter play. Always bidding everything goes broke on the first lot and buys nothing afterwards. Always offering 3 cards hands rivals large, efficient lots. Talk is left out. Interests do conflict, but in a sealed-bid auction the main use of talk is proposing that everyone bid low, a cartel that strips out the pricing decision. Bluffing about favoured goods is already carried by the bids themselves, which are costly signals rather than cheap talk.

balanced.evidence:
CARD VALUES: each good runs 0,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,5,5, so the sum is 33 and the mean is 2.75. A full 5-card ship averages about 13.75. A 3-card lot ranges from 0 to 15.

REWARD POOL: The day prizes are 15 + 7 = 22 per day, so 66 over the game. Majorities pay 4 x 10 = 40. The favoured good pays 3 per card, and there are 12 cards of each good per day. With 3 players, ship capacity is 3 x 5 x 3 = 45 cards out of the 54 revealed.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE (most florins):
(a) Always pass (bid 0). Final total is 40, with no rewards. Two sensible rivals share 66 + 40 + about 12-24 in favoured bonuses, roughly 60-65 each. Each can spend up to about 20 and still finish above 40. With only two bidders, the second-place 7 is near-guaranteed to anyone holding a nonzero ship, so lots go cheaply. Result: pass LOSES to sensible play. Against random bidders (uniform 0..florins), the random player spends about half its money per lot and goes broke within 2-3 wins. Pass can beat random play but not sensible play, so it is not a never-lose policy.
(b) Always bid the maximum. It wins lot 1 for 40 florins and then can only bid 0. Final is about 0 + 15 at best + perhaps one majority, under 40. It loses to everyone.
(c) Always bid 1. It wins only lots that everyone else values at 0, and loses every contested lot. It rarely tops ship value and loses to sensible play.
(d) Always choose lot size 1 (or 3) as active player. This is a weak fixed habit. Lot size interacts with the 5-card cap: a size-3 lot blocks any player holding 3 or more cards. No size is dominant.

STRICT DOMINANCE: No bid level or lot size is better regardless of others. It is a first-price sealed bid with capacity and majority externalities, so the value of a lot depends on rivals' ships and suspected favoured goods.

SEAT EDGE: There are 2N rounds per day, so each seat is active exactly twice per day and 6 times per game. Every day restarts at seat 1, which is symmetric. The active player's powers are the lot size and tie priority. Late-day active turns are slightly weaker because ships are fuller, but every seat gets one early and one late slot per day. The edge is minor.

INFORMATION: Everyone sees the same lots, winners and prices. The only asymmetry is a privately known favoured good, which is dealt symmetrically.

PAYOFF LABELS: The 15/7 split, the tied-first split of 22 (11 for 2, 7 for 3, 5 for 4) and the 10 per majority are arithmetically consistent as described. Any player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS:
- Deck: fully specified at 48 cards. Each day uses at most 3 x 8 = 24 cards, so the deck never runs out.
- Active seat: given by formula.
- Lot: fixed as a prefix of A,B,C.
- Bids: simultaneous, from 0 to current florins.
- Overfill rule: invalidates the bid.
- Ties: the active player first, then seating order after the active player.
- All-zero bids: the lot is discarded.
- Day scoring: covers a tied first (no second paid), a tied second, and zero-value ships.
- Reset: ships empty, good counts persist.
- End scoring: majorities with split ties, favoured bonus.
- Winner: florins, then total cards, then a draw.
- Full ships: such a player's bids are simply invalid, which is handled by step 4.
I found no unresolved situation.

FINITE: Play is fixed at 18 or 24 rounds, and the result is pure arithmetic on tracked numbers.

LIMITS: steps 16 <= 20, choice steps 2 <= 4 (lot size, then a simultaneous bid poll), attributes 14 <= 20, hidden 2 <= 3, rounds 24 <= 40.

RANDOM DRAWS: The only random operation is one shuffle at the start of each day. The reveal is a remove/append from the list, which is the supported workaround. So at most 1 random draw per round.

NO UNSUPPORTED FEATURES: no board, judge, clock, trading or binding agreements. Bids are a simultaneous poll, as required.

TALK: Its absence is defensible. Inference comes from public lots, winners and prices, so players are not merely guessing. Talk would mostly invite non-binding bid-rigging chatter.

NOTE: 'Private' florin totals can be reconstructed exactly from public prices and computable day and majority awards. This is a memory and inference task, not true hiddenness. It is acceptable but should not be counted as a meaningful hidden element.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE ELEMENTS: the daily shuffle, which all players see equally, and the favoured-good deal, which is symmetric (each good equally likely, 12 cards each).

WHAT DECIDES THE WINNER:
- Bid shading in a first-price sealed auction.
- Valuing a lot against your remaining capacity, the day race for 15/7 and the 10-point majorities.
- Inferring rivals' favoured goods from what they pay premiums for. The favoured good is worth 3 per card, roughly half a mean card's worth extra.
- Tracking rivals' exact florins from public prices.
- As active player, choosing a lot size that blocks rivals near capacity or denies them a key good.

GOOD-PLAY OUTCOME: When all players play well, the favoured-good deal does not by itself pick the winner, because every player gets one good with an identical distribution. Lot order varies, but every player sees and bids on every lot, so luck is shared rather than private.

ESTIMATE: chance is about 25-35% of outcome variance, from lot sequencing relative to active turns. Reasoning-driven bidding should clearly beat naive or random bidding: random bidders bankrupt themselves, and passive players forfeit roughly 60 florins of rewards. There is real hidden information to infer and act on: favoured goods and remaining money.
